'''Emma Parmee'''  is a British chemist and research scientist who is a co-inventor of numerous drug patents. She was one of the leading researchers in the development of [[sitagliptin]] and was awarded a Thomas Alva Edison Patent Award in 2007 and the [[Society of Chemical Industry (American Section)|Society of Chemical Industry]]'s [[Gordon E. Moore Medal (SCI)|Gordon E Moore Medal]] in 2009 for her contributions.<ref name="CFOH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Emma R. Parmee |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/parmee-emma-r|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref>

==Biography==
Emma Rachel Parmee was born in the United Kingdom obtaining a BA and PhD at the [[University of Oxford]] in chemistry.<ref name=symposium>{{cite web|title=12th Annual Maria Goeppert-Mayer Interdisciplinary Symposium|url=http://www.chem.uzh.ch/static/events/mgm/Archive2005.html|publisher=University of Zurich|accessdate=19 November 2015|location=Zurich, Switzerland|year=2006}}</ref> She completed her thesis in 1990<ref name=Thesis>{{cite web|title=Synthesis of avermectins and milbemycins| date=1990 |url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.258233|publisher=British Library|accessdate=19 November 2015 | last1=Rachel. | first1=Parmee }}</ref> and was awarded a NATO post-doctoral fellowship. She moved to the United States to complete her post-doctoral work under [[Saturo Masamune]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], studying [[catalysts]] of [[asymmetric synthesis]] for [[aldol reaction]]s. She completed her post-doctoral research in 1992 and joined [[Merck & Co.]] that same year working at their research laboratory in [[Rahway, New Jersey]].<ref name=symposium />

In 2006, Parmee was one of the lead investigators in the discovery of the selective [[Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor]] [[sitagliptin]] (marketed by Merck under the trade name '''Januvia'''). The drug is used to treat [[Diabetes mellitus type 2|Type 2 Diabetes]] and provides glucose lowering benefits without the side effects of some of the previously available treatments.<ref name="2009 Medal">{{cite web|title=Emma Parmee Gordon E Moore 2009 Medalist|url=http://www.soci.org/news/awards/gordon-e-moore/awards-gordon-e-moore-parmee|publisher=Society of Chemical Industry|accessdate=19 November 2015|location=London, England|year=2009}}</ref> Her involvement was recognised by the award of the Thomas Alva Edison Patent Award from the [[Research and Development Council of New Jersey]],<ref name="TAE award">{{cite journal|title=The Research & Development Council of New Jersey 2007 Thomas Alva Edison Patent Awards |journal=Cosmetiscope |date=December 2007 |volume=13 |issue=10 |page=10 |publisher=New York Society of Cosmetic Chemists |location=Mt. Freedom, New Jersey }}</ref> the Prix Galien<ref name="Prix Galien recipient">{{cite web|title=31st Annual Tribute to Women and Industry Awards Dinner|url=http://journals.eventjournal.com/view_custom.php?journal_id=205&id=18558|publisher=YWCA of Central New Jersey|accessdate=19 November 2015|location=Plainfield, New Jersey|date=26 May 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160216124344/http://journals.eventjournal.com/view_custom.php?journal_id=205&id=18558|archive-date=16 February 2016|url-status=usurped}}</ref> for Endocrinology in 2007<ref name="2007 Prix Galien">{{cite web|title=Winners Sorted by Medical Field|url=http://www.prixgalien.com/en/05/02/winners-sorted-by-medical-field.htm|publisher=Prix Galien|accessdate=19 November 2015|location=Neuilly sur Seine, France|year=2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151104120152/http://www.prixgalien.com/en/05/02/winners-sorted-by-medical-field.htm|archive-date=4 November 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the receipt of the 2009 Gordon E Moore Medal from the Society of Chemical Industry.<ref name="2009 Medal" />

In 2010, Parmee left the Rahway lab and moved to the facility at [[West Point, Pennsylvania]], where she served as the site lead for chemical discovery until 2013. Her group developed a small molecule CGRP antagonist.<ref name="CGRP molecule">{{cite journal|title=Emma Parmee, Vice President, Discovery Chemistry, Merck|journal=Industry Matters Newsletter |date= 9 July 2020 |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/industry/industry-matters/boss-talk/emma-parmee.html?sc=200723_sc_twitter_indnews_bosstalk|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=26 March 2021}}</ref> She was then promoted to Associate Vice-President and Head of Exploratory Chemistry . She also serves as the co-chair of the Early Discovery Council for Merck Research Laboratories.   She has written more than forty papers which have appeared in peer-reviewed publications and has filed for over thirty US patents on her work.<ref name="move to Pennsylvania">{{cite web|title=Dr. Emma R. Parmee|url=http://projects.iq.harvard.edu/bostonwincs/people/industry-speaker|publisher=Harvard University|accessdate=19 November 2015|location=Boston, Massachusetts|year=2015}}</ref> Parmee lives with her husband, son, and daughter.
